RESPONSE_TO: CC2
0.50 findings/Kchar is not supportable as a protocol-only expectation from the supplied data. My independent observation: baseline overall efficiency in Exp 31 is 360 / 1260 = 0.286 findings/Kchar, and cross-model references are only 2.9% of tokens. Even if that entire slice were compressed to near-zero, the ceiling gain from verdict compression alone is trivial. A move into ~0.35-0.42 is evidence-based from format compression plus dedup/closure; >=0.50 requires an additional assumption that churn drops sharply and that models materially shorten finding bodies, which is not demonstrated by the protocol data alone. Definitive stance: 0.50+ is possible only with both protocol discipline and actual duplicate suppression; overhead elimination alone is insufficient.

RESPONSE_TO: DeepSeek
Your ~15% social overhead estimate is plausible as a hypothesis, but it is not directly measured in the artifact. My independent observation is stronger and narrower: the artifact explicitly says only 2.9% of tokens were cross-model references, so the dominant waste cannot be missing verdict compression alone. The larger waste is duplicated and malformed finding bodies: 58.3% churn, 100% wrong FFF ordering, and unstable IDs. Definitive stance: social overhead exists, but the evidence supports structured finding compression and duplicate closure as the primary levers.

CONFIRM ChatGPT_F001
CONFIRM ChatGPT_F002
CONFIRM ChatGPT_F003
CHALLENGE CC2_F001 | The 15-25% social-overhead share is not measured in the artifact, while 58.3% churn and 100% FFF-order failure are measured. Social overhead may matter, but calling it the primary compressible waste is under-evidenced.
CHALLENGE CC2_F003 | Mandatory verdict on every prior finding is likely excessive and unsupported by the artifact. With 5 models and many findings, this can inflate token volume. The evidence supports mandatory verdicts on addressed messages and on overlapping findings, not universal all-to-all verdicting.
CHALLENGE DeepSeek_D001R1 | Your proposed stable ID format includes round suffixes (e.g. C001R1). That violates the stated requirement that finding IDs are unique across the entire experiment and never reused; embedding round in the identifier incentivizes round-local identity and breaks persistence across rounds.
CHALLENGE DeepSeek_D002R1 | The efficiency uplift is overclaimed. Starting from 0.286 findings/Kchar, a 72-124% increase to 0.50-0.65 is not justified by the observed levers, especially when cross-model references are only 2.9% of tokens and social overhead is unmeasured.
EXTEND Gemini_F002 | The sentence "eliminating the 97.1% of tokens that are non-reference conversational filler" is not supported by the data. 97.1% means "not cross-model references," not "filler." Most of that mass is finding content. The protocol target should be compressing finding structure and suppressing duplicates, not treating all non-reference text as waste.
MERGE ChatGPT_F002 <- F001
MERGE ChatGPT_F004 <- F003

Final synthesis: the strongest evidence supports a compact structured-finding protocol with stable experiment-global IDs, evidence-backed CHALLENGE, and closure semantics. The main waste in Exp 31 was not the tiny cross-model reference slice but duplicate and malformed finding bodies. I reject round-encoded IDs, universal all-to-all verdict requirements, and optimistic 0.50-0.65 efficiency claims as under-evidenced. The evidence-based prediction is a moderate gain: roughly 22% fewer characters, about 0.37 findings/Kchar overall, and modestly faster convergence rather than a guaranteed gamma crossing. Definitive stance: lock the protocol in F002 and evaluate it with both overall and novelty-aware efficiency metrics.
